They Criticized eBay. Then the Harassment Started.
They Criticized eBay. Then the Harassment Started.
eBay Employees Targeted Two Critics. Then It Got Worse.
View test report
Edit title
Description
In 2019, a campaign run by people working in or with eBay’s security organization targeted EcommerceBytes publishers Ina and David Steiner with disturbing deliveries, online harassment, surveillance, and an attempted GPS-tracker installation.

This documentary follows how criticism of eBay moved through internal messages and corporate security, how all seven federally prosecuted participants pleaded guilty, why eBay later entered a deferred prosecution agreement and paid a separate $3 million criminal penalty, and how the civil case ultimately ended in a $55.7 million settlement package in July 2026.

Important legal distinction: the $55.7 million figure was a civil settlement package — not a judgment and not an eBay-only payment. The separate $3 million DPA penalty is not included in that total. Claims that survived summary judgment were not final findings of liability, and the civil case settled without a jury verdict on those questions.

CHAPTERS
00:00 A Package From eBay
01:15 Two Publishers and a Global Marketplace
02:11 The Temperature Rises
03:39 When Reputation Becomes Security
04:44 The Operation
05:57 The Second Problem
06:57 Seven Guilty Pleas
07:57 eBay Gets Its Own Criminal Case
09:31 How High Did Responsibility Go?
11:50 The Settlement That Didn’t Settle It
12:38 What It Cost
14:05 The Cost of Turning Criticism Into an Operation

Adobe Paid $1 Billion for a Deal That Never Happened
Adobe’s Failed Figma Deal Cost $1 Billion
Adobe’s Failed Figma Deal Cost $1 Billion
View test report
Edit title
Description
Adobe agreed to buy Figma for about $20 billion. The acquisition never closed. Adobe still paid Figma $1 billion.

That billion dollars was not a government fine. It came from a reverse termination fee the two companies negotiated before the merger agreement was signed. This episode follows the record — SEC filings, the merger agreement, UK CMA and European Commission documents — to show how the clause entered the deal, why the regulators' concerns grew, how the deal ended by mutual termination before any final UK or EU prohibition, and how three business days later the clause became cash.

CHAPTERS
00:00 A Billion Dollars for a Deal That Never Closed
00:53 The Twenty-Billion-Dollar Bet
02:11 The Clause Existed Before the Deal
03:50 What a Reverse Termination Fee Actually Does
04:46 Then the Deal Became Public
05:38 The Reviews Expand
07:00 The Concerns Become Hard to Ignore
08:22 Adobe and Figma Push Back
09:42 The Deal Ends Before the Final “No”
11:03 Three Days Later, the Contract Fires
12:10 The Two Numbers People Confuse
13:15 Figma After Adobe
14:28 What the Clause Was Really Pricing

The Lawsuit That Could Break DistroKid
DistroKid’s AI Music Nightmare
DistroKid’s AI Music Nightmare
View test report
Edit title
Description
Universal Music Group sued DistroKid — but the most important part of the case is not simply whether AI music is legal.

The complaint targets the company in the middle: the distributor that moves uploads from creators to streaming platforms. This documentary examines UMG's allegations, DistroKid's public response, disputed recording identifiers, copyright notices, the complaint's large track counts, and why the frequently repeated $150,000 figure is not the automatic value of the lawsuit.

The central question is bigger than one upload: when does a distributor's own conduct become part of the copyright dispute?

As of October 5, 2026, the allegations remain disputed. The reviewed public docket showed no merits ruling, damages award or injunction. Nothing in this video should be understood as a finding that any defendant is liable.

CHAPTERS
00:00 4,562 tracks and one unexpected defendant
00:55 What DistroKid actually does
02:25 Why this is not simply “AI music is illegal”
03:59 1,000 examples are not 1,000 court findings
05:25 The tiny code behind a recording
06:58 Why a rights notice changes the story
08:31 DistroKid says Universal has it wrong
09:57 Why $150,000 per work is not the lawsuit's value
11:30 The timing around the fight
12:22 The case is young
13:20 What Universal is asking the court to test
14:39 The pipe is now the battleground

VISUAL DISCLOSURE
This documentary combines authentic public documents, company material, custom explanatory graphics, and AI-generated illustrative reconstructions. Reconstructions are illustrative and are not presented as original documents or footage.

This video is an independent documentary and is not affiliated with or sponsored by Universal Music Group, DistroKid, any streaming platform, or any party to the litigation. It is provided for informational and commentary purposes and is not legal advice.
